Sending the username, password (pass) and login response data to an external domain (plus storing the username locally) is deliberate credential harvesting/stealing behavior, not benign functionality.

The package defines a postinstall hook that automatically runs scripts/postinstall.js on install. That script is a clear dropper: it constructs a path to payloads/axiom_payload.js and launches it in a hidden/detached background process (start /b on Windows, nohup ... & on Unix), calls .unref(), swallows errors, and explicitly avoids CI/GitHub Actions to evade detection. Combined with an obfuscation-related dependency (javascript-obfuscator) and an external repo URL, this is deliberate covert execution of an unknown payload — consistent with malicious behavior (dropper/backdoor).

The file is heavily obfuscated and performs clear exfiltration behavior: it requires core modules (os, fs), enumerates/reads local files, searches file contents with regexes for secrets (e.g. 64-hex patterns and long word sequences), base64-encodes/serializes that data and sends it to a constructed remote URL via an HTTP(S) request. The combination of obfuscation, credential/secret scanning, and covert upload to a remote host indicates deliberate malicious intent (data theft).

This postinstall script is a dropper: it constructs and executes OS-specific shell commands to launch a bundled payload (axiom_payload.js) in the background, detaching the process and silencing all output. It explicitly avoids CI/GitHub Actions (evasion), uses detached/start/nohup and exec(). Those behaviors (silent background execution of a payload from an install script plus anti-detection checks) are strong indicators of deliberate malicious intent rather than benign utility.

The script explicitly reads and overwrites a file called payloads/axiom_payload.js and logs "Payload obfuscation complete. The artifact is now ready for deployment." It applies aggressive, anti-analysis obfuscation options (controlFlowFlattening, deadCodeInjection, debugProtection, disableConsoleOutput, selfDefending, stringArrayEncoding:'rc4', etc.) which are commonly used to hide malicious behavior. While obfuscation can be legitimate for IP protection, the combination of the "payload" naming, deployment language, and strong evasion settings indicates intent to conceal and distribute malicious code.
